name: Jwalamukhi Temple, Kangra
deity: The Goddess as Jwalamukhi (Jwala Devi, Vaishnavi), worshipped as nine natural flames
period: Ancient Shakti shrine of the Kangra hills, named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram and recorded in a 14th-century chronicle; present building shaped by later royal patrons
dynasty: Katoch kings of Kangra (by tradition), with later gifts from the Sikh court of Lahore
style: North Indian Himalayan, with a gilded dome and silver-plated doors
summary: Jwalamukhi is the Shakti Peetha of the burning goddess, where no idol stands and the tongue of Sati is remembered in flames that rise from the living rock of the Kangra hills and are said never to go out.

sections.history: Jwalamukhi lies in the green foothills of the Kangra valley, and its worship is older than any building that now stands there. The Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha stotram, traditionally ascribed to Adi Shankara, names the place in the line Jwalayam Vaishnavi and counts it among the eighteen great seats of the Goddess; tradition holds that here the tongue of Sati fell to earth. Local memory credits Bhumi Chand of the Katoch line, the ruler of Kangra and a devotee of Durga, with first raising a shrine after a dream led him to the spot. A Persian chronicle of the fourteenth century records the visit of Firuz Shah Tughlaq to the place during his Kangra campaign, and later rulers, among them the Sikh court at Lahore, added to the shrine. Through every age the devotion has stayed fixed on the same flames.
sections.architecture: There is no image in the sanctum. The shrine is a compact hall of North Indian hill style, crowned by a gilded dome and several small pinnacles and entered through silver-plated doors, with a small pillared hall before it. Inside, flames rise from fissures in the rock, nine of them counted and honoured as nine forms of the Goddess, among them Mahakali, Annapurna, Chandi, Hinglaj, Vindhyavasini, Mahalakshmi, Saraswati, Ambika and Anji Devi. The principal flame, burning from a hollowed rock, is regarded as the mouth of the Goddess herself, and devotees offer to the fire as to a living presence. Close above the shrine stands the Gorakh Dibbi, a place of the Nath yogis where a pool appears to boil because gas rises through its water.
sections.legends: The foundation story is that of Sati. When she gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice and Shiva wandered with her body, her limbs fell across the land, and here, tradition says, her tongue fell and became the fire; Unmatta Bhairava keeps the place as her guardian. Local tradition adds the story of the Mughal emperor Akbar. He is said to have tried to quench the flames with an iron disc and with a channel of water, and when the fire would not yield he came to the shrine and offered a golden umbrella, which turned into an unknown metal in his hands. This is told as oral tradition and is not found in the Mughal court records, but it is the tale that pilgrims carry home. A story of the Nath saint Gorakhnath, who set a pot to boil and promised to return, explains the boiling pool beside the temple.
sections.festivals: The great gatherings are the two Navratri seasons, in Chaitra (March or April) and Ashwin (September or October), when fairs fill the streets around the shrine and pilgrims arrive from across northern India. Aarti is offered several times a day, from the waking of the Goddess at dawn through the evening aarti to the Shayan aarti that lays her to rest. Confirm dates and aarti times locally, as the festivals follow the lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Jwalamukhi without expecting an image. Climb the lane to the gilded dome, pass through the silver doors, and stand before the small flames at the rock, whose light seems quieter and steadier than any lamp lit by hand. Many pilgrims offer sweet prasad and sit afterwards in the courtyard to watch the aarti. Walk on to the Gorakh Dibbi above the temple for the view over the valley. Queues grow long during Navratri, so an early weekday morning gives the most unhurried darshan.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to late evening, with a closure of about an hour around midday; hours differ between summer and winter, and aarti times are fixed. Confirm timings locally, especially during Navratri.
visit.dressCode: Modest attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the stands near the entrance, and warm clothing is useful in the cooler months.
visit.photography: Photography is usually restricted inside the sanctum and near the flames; outer courtyards are generally more relaxed. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals, priests or other devotees.
visit.gettingThere: Jwalamukhi is a town in Kangra district of Himachal Pradesh, roughly 50 km by road from Dharamshala. Gaggal airport at Kangra is about 45 to 50 km away, and Pathankot, the main broad-gauge railhead, is about 110 to 125 km away. Jwalamukhi Road, on the Kangra Valley narrow-gauge line, is the nearest station. Buses and taxis serve the town, and the temple is a short walk from the bus stand.
